Review target: `fix/degraded-results-are-not-kept`

`high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates are the dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity.

## Output

Target **at least 5 findings**. If fewer genuine findings exist, emit what you have — do not invent to hit the floor.

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives, return `[]`. Do not call the
ReportFindings tool even if it is available - this review's
output contract is the JSON block above.

+/// Answers that go out in a batch with others: what [`Answers`] keeps for a question asked alone. A caller takes each
+/// question it needs ([`BatchAnswers::take`]), sends the ones it was given as one request, answers them, and only then
+/// waits for the ones another caller was given, so a wait is never for an answer that waits on one of ours. A question
+/// whose asker failed is not kept: whoever waited for it takes it on the next round.
+pub(crate) struct BatchAnswers<K, V> {
+    slots: Mutex<FxHashMap<K, Arc<Slot<V>>>>,
+}
+
+struct Slot<V> {
+    answer: OnceLock<V>,
+    /// Held by the one caller asking this question.
+    asking: Arc<AsyncMutex<()>>,
+}
+
+/// What [`BatchAnswers::take`] says about a question.
+pub(crate) enum Taken<V> {
+    /// Answered: [`BatchAnswers::peek`] has it.
+    Kept,
+    /// Nobody is asking it, and the caller now is: it must [`Mine::answer`] it, or drop it to leave it unanswered.
+    Mine(Mine<V>),
+    /// Another caller is asking it.
+    Theirs(Theirs),
+}
+
+/// A question the caller is asking.
+pub(crate) struct Mine<V> {
+    slot: Arc<Slot<V>>,
+    _asking: OwnedMutexGuard<()>,
+}
+
+/// A question another caller is asking.
+pub(crate) struct Theirs(Arc<AsyncMutex<()>>);
+
+impl<K, V> Default for BatchAnswers<K, V> {
+    fn default() -> Self {
+        BatchAnswers { slots: Mutex::default() }

---
cargo/caliper-docgen-core: minor
cargo/caliper-docgen: patch
cargo/caliper-docgen-napi: patch
npm/caliper-docgen: patch
---

**A checker outage or an unreadable dependency file no longer sticks to a component.** The next request or run asks again and gets the real answer.

- Why it matters: in a watch or Storybook session, one checker timeout, crash or rejected request used to leave the component on its structural props until a source file changed, and a rejected request was also kept on disk as the checker's answer. A dependency `.d.ts` that could not be read once (too many open files, an install racing the run) used to be kept as "not exported", in the session until it restarted and in the dependency index for later runs.
- What you see now: every answer the failed checker affects carries its warning. The component is asked again 30 seconds later or after the next source-file change; until then a request gets the structural props and the warning at once, without waiting on a checker that just failed. A run that cannot read a dependency file still warns, and keeps everything it could read: a type a later `export *` target declares, and the React augmentations of the other files. The session's next request and the next run read the file again, and once it reads, the component has its full props and the warning is gone.
- Also covered: a prop that a package's type inherits from another file of the package that could not be read, and a generic component (`as` props) whose instantiation the checker rejected. Each is asked again on the next request instead of being kept without the prop.
- A file that stays unreadable is reported once in each answer, however many requests a session makes.

**Breaking:** for Rust users of `caliper-docgen-core`, `SemanticOutcome` has a new field `unavailable` (set only by `SemanticOutcome::unavailable`) and `SemanticFallback` a new field `transient`. A struct literal that names every field no longer compiles: add `unavailable: None` and `transient: false`, or build the outcome with `..Default::default()`.
diff --git a/docs/performance.md b/docs/performance.md
index 17bd6212..69a8f18f 100644
--- a/docs/performance.md
+++ b/docs/performance.md
@@ -4,6 +4,40 @@ How fast Caliper is and what it costs is recorded in `docs/measurement.md`: a we
 
 The per-pull-request scorecard that used to enforce these numbers is gone. It caught one real regression (Mantine 38% and Chakra 47% slower after a batch of 20 resolver pull requests merged on 2026-10-26, found by the weekly run), and its gates failed on runner noise and on bases that had moved. The figures below came from it and are history, not limits.
 
+## Results with the checker and dependencies, 2026-11-23
+
+What a user gets by default: the checker and `--load-dependencies` on. The 15 to 39 times of the 2026-10-22 table below is the structural resolver alone; with the checker the edge over react-docgen-typescript (RDT) is 2 to 9 times cold and 6 to 30 times on a second run.
+
+Method: `scripts/weekly.py` (no `--oracle`) on main at `f00cbdc4`, five runs per corpus, Apple Silicon laptop, macOS, load average 8 to 12. Cold is one whole process; second run is the same command with the cache warm. RDT is the same run through `withCustomConfig`.
+
+| Corpus   | Caliper cold | Caliper second run |    RDT | Cold vs RDT | Second run vs RDT | Peak RSS, Caliper / RDT |
+| -------- | -----------: | -----------------: | -----: | ----------: | ----------------: | ----------------------: |
+| mantine  |       0.82 s |             0.32 s | 1.88 s |        2.3× |              5.8× |           645 / 583 MiB |
+| chakra   |       2.92 s |             0.94 s | 26.5 s |        9.1× |               28× |       1,077 / 2,865 MiB |
+| shadcn   |       1.39 s |             0.67 s |  5.0 s |        3.6× |              7.4× |         715 / 1,612 MiB |
+| antd     |       0.77 s |             0.10 s | 3.05 s |        4.0× |               30× |         367 / 1,070 MiB |
+| spectrum |       0.59 s |             0.27 s | 2.69 s |        4.5× |              9.9× |           456 / 876 MiB |
+
+Caliper's peak memory is below RDT's on four corpora and above it on Mantine.
+
+Since 2026-11-19 the cold runs fell by the whole-program diagnostics fix (`getSemanticDiagnostics` was sent `file`, which tsrs ignores, so every cold run type-checked the whole program: 12 to 76% wall time), by fewer and deduplicated checker requests, and by one conversion of an identical type instead of several in parallel.
+
+### Where the CPU goes, 2026-11-23
+
+A cold run makes about 40 threads: two rayon pools of 18 (Caliper's and tsrs's own `worker_pool()`, which tsrs sizes only from `RAYON_NUM_THREADS`), four tokio converter threads, two checker threads and main. `sample` at 1 ms on shadcn (load 3.7): about 37% of on-CPU samples are file-system syscalls, which is why system time is about 35% of CPU (user 3.5 s, sys 2.2 s). The largest items are tsrs's `realpath` (an `lstat` per path component), `read_file` and `file_exists`; Caliper's own dependency loader and `resolve_package_types_file` account for about 260 samples. Rayon idle spinning is about 4% on a quiet machine and about 30% at load 32.
+
+Variants, five interleaved runs on a quiet machine (output byte-identical in every one):
+
+| Variant | Wall | CPU | Peak RSS |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `RAYON_NUM_THREADS=4` (both pools) | -2% to +12%, Chakra +7% (+23% at 2 threads) | -20% to -39% | -5% to -16% |
+| tsrs pool at 4, Caliper's unchanged | unchanged | -4% to -30% | 0 to -5% |
+| Caliper's pool at 4, tsrs's unchanged | +5% to +9% on four corpora | -6% to -15% | -5% to -10% |
+| One checker program (`CHECKER_PROGRAMS = 1`) | -2% to +20% (Mantine +20%) | -13% to -21% | -2% to -5% |
+| Two converter threads | -9% to +19% | -7% to 0% | unchanged |
+
+A thread cap costs wall time and the addon's session start (`startMs` 63 to 67 ms became 89 to 91 ms with Caliper's pool at 4), so it is not applied. The cap that costs nothing is on tsrs's pool, which needs a setting from tsrs.
+
 ## Size model
 
 Extraction time fits t ≈ 6.4 ms + 0.13 ms/kLOC + 3.8 ms/kprop (props summed over components). It is a sizing guide, reported by the old scorecard as "Model ms", never a gate: a fixed cost that varies by machine dominates small corpora, so per-corpus residuals vary too much to gate on. On the run below the model is within 2× of the measured extract time on every corpus (0.45× for mantine to 1.6× for chakra).
diff --git a/docs/releasing.md b/docs/releasing.md
